items.title: Support-surface debt authorization is not scoped by target or upstream version

prompt: Work item: uaa-0046 — a debt row's authorization carries no target and no upstream version, so it can absorb obligations it was never granted for.

`SurfaceIdentity` is `(surface_kind, command_path, surface_id)` with `command_path` rooted at the agent id (`crates/xtask/src/agent_maintenance/support_audit.rs`). Agent, command path, item kind and surface leaf all participate. Target does not, and neither does upstream version.

Two consequences. A deferral authorized while only Linux was acquired matches a newly appearing Windows gap for the same command and flag, so the old authorization silently covers the new target. And loading a new version's report does not re-authorize an old debt decision — the upstream version selects which report is read and is validated against report metadata, but it never constrains whether a debt row still applies.

This is compounded by the audit preferring `coverage.any.json`. The reporter's `any` resolution treats coverage on any relevant target as presence (`crates/xtask/src/manifest_report/wrapper.rs`), so the obligation set the audit derives is already an aggregate that can omit a target-specific gap. Adding target fields to the debt inventory alone does not fix that, because the gaps being matched would still come from the aggregate.
Distinct from `uaa-0041`. That item is about surface *semantics* — accepted values, arity, output shape. This one is about *authorization scope*. Neither covers the other.

The any-report/union-target equality check added on 2026-09-15 does not close this: it runs only in unmatched-debt classification (`support_audit/unmatched_debt.rs`), and adds no scope to matched debt authorizations.

Trigger — resolve before the first of: (1) a target is added to any agent's `union.expected_targets`; (2) closeout begins enforcing `uaa-0039`, which reads the same authorizations. Pointers: the Surface identity rules in `docs/specs/maintenance-request-contract-v1.md`, and the `uaa-0041` row it must not be merged into.
Steps:

1) Decide where applicability lives: on the debt row, in the identity key, or both. A durable row may legitimately apply across versions, but that must be stated, not inherited from a global name match.
2) Freeze the currently authorized target set during migration. An omitted scope must not be read as 'whatever targets RULES.json later contains'.
3) Derive target-specific obligations from the per-target reports that acquisition already produces, rather than from the any-report aggregate.
4) Add a test where a new target introduces a gap that an existing single-target deferral must not absorb.
deliverables: A decision on where target and version applicability is recorded
The migration's frozen target set
Target-specific obligations derived from per-target evidence
A test binding a new target against an existing deferral

notes: Recorded 2026-09-16 from a ChatGPT Pro review of a bounded repository bundle at `b8e3722e`. Pro raised it and stated explicitly that `uaa-0041` does not already cover it; verified against the identity construction and the any-report resolution.

items.title: Permission-test fixtures restore the directory mode only on the success path

prompt: Work item: uaa-0047 — two permission fixtures in `crates/xtask/tests/agent_maintenance_audit_status.rs` leak a modified directory mode when their body does not return normally.

`run_with_unreadable_evidence` (around line 733) chmods the coverage report directory to `0000`, then calls `expect_err` on the audit, and only restores the mode after that call returns. Under an identity that bypasses permission checks the audit succeeds, `expect_err` panics, and the directory stays at `0000` for the remainder of the test binary — so later tests in the same process fail for a reason unrelated to what they assert.
`with_unwritable_emit_parent` (around line 724) has the same shape: it sets `0555` on the emit parent and restores only after `action()` returns.

Both fixtures are `#[cfg(unix)]`, not root-gated, so today they fail rather than skip under a permission-bypassing identity. That is the correct failure direction; the risk is introducing a skip that asks the code under test whether the environment enforces permissions, which would let a real regression read as an environmental skip.

Related work already in flight: the root-safe permission-test effort the 2026-09-15 ChatGPT Pro review asked for — probe the fixture independently of the code under test, restore on every exit path including the skip path, keep mandatory unprivileged coverage. This row exists so the restoration defect does not depend on that effort being picked up.

Size constraint: the file is 695 code lines against the repository's 700-line cap, so a guard type and an independent probe cannot be added in place. It needs a split first, and `make loc-check` must pass afterwards.
Trigger — resolve before the first of: (1) the root-safe permission-test work starts; (2) any new case is added to this file. Pointer: the two helpers named above.
Steps:
1) Split the file so there is room under the 700-code-line cap.
2) Replace both restore calls with a guard type whose `Drop` restores the original mode, installed immediately after the mode is changed, so returns, assertion failures and unwinding all restore.

3) Probe the fixture with a direct filesystem operation before asserting on the audit: permission denied establishes the fixture, success means this environment cannot exercise the test, any other error is a fixture failure rather than a skip.
4) Keep the unprivileged CI lane mandatory, where failing to establish denial fails the job.
deliverables: The file split under the 700-code-line cap
A Drop-based restoration guard on both fixtures
An independent fixture probe that distinguishes denial, non-enforcement and fixture failure
Mandatory unprivileged coverage retained

notes: Recorded 2026-09-16 from a ChatGPT Pro review of a bounded repository bundle at `b8e3722e`. Verified by reading both helpers; the 695-of-700 measurement is from tokei.

items.title: The nightly watcher regenerates and force-pushes an open packet branch, so nothing committed to it survives until merge

prompt: Work item: uaa-0048 — the nightly watcher regenerates and force-pushes an open packet branch, so nothing committed to it survives until merge.

Context: `.github/workflows/agent-maintenance-release-watch.yml` runs on `cron: "17 3 * * *"` and its `queue` job compares the repository's validated pointer against upstream latest. The pointer only advances at promotion, which happens after closeout and merge, so an open packet still reads as needed every night. The queue has no dedupe against an already-open packet PR, and the dispatch step calls `createWorkflowDispatch` unconditionally for every queued row.

Each dispatch runs `agent-maintenance-open-pr.yml`, which regenerates the packet with `prepare-agent-maintenance --request-recorded-at "$(date -u ...)"` and calls `peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8` with `add-paths: <maintenance root>` and `body-path: docs/agents/lifecycle/<agent>-maintenance/governance/pr-summary.md`. The action resets the packet branch to `staging`, re-applies the packet as one commit, and force-pushes. The `acquire` job then re-adds its own commit.

Evidence (read-only `gh`, 2026-09-19): PR #211 was created 2026-09-16 and PR #208 on 2026-09-15; neither agent's target version changed in the interval (claude_code has been on 2.1.267 for four days, opencode on 1.18.30 for five). Both PRs carry exactly two commits, all four dated 2026-09-19 08:03-08:08. No commit from either PR's creation day still exists, so the branch history is replaced nightly on an unchanged target version. The watcher produced three `agent-maintenance-open-pr` runs per night on each of 2026-09-15 through 2026-09-19.

Why it blocks T8: the lifecycle spec requires a packet be closed on its own branch before merge, so the merge carries a closed HANDOFF. `close-agent-maintenance` writes the closeout artifact and regenerates HANDOFF inside the packet's maintenance root, which is exactly the `add-paths` tree the nightly run regenerates and force-pushes. A closeout committed during the day is therefore overwritten at the next run, with HANDOFF regenerated back to the open-run contributor contract. That is the same wrong-HANDOFF end state the spec records for the merged-open codex packet (#153), reached by a different route. Not yet observed directly: no closeout has been run against a live packet.
Steps:

1) Decide the stand-down condition: a closeout artifact present in the packet, a maintainer label, PR ready-for-review, or an explicit freeze marker. Prefer a condition the packet itself carries, so the watcher needs no external state.
2) Implement it in the `queue` job or as an early guard in `agent-maintenance-open-pr.yml`, so a stood-down packet is neither regenerated nor re-acquired.
3) Decide what the watcher should do when a stood-down packet's upstream version is superseded, since `Close superseded same-agent PRs` would otherwise close a packet a maintainer is mid-closeout on.
4) Confirm directly, before relying on either answer, whether a closeout committed to a packet branch is in fact destroyed by the next nightly run.
5) Add a contract test for the stand-down condition.
Output: a packet a maintainer has begun closing is not regenerated, re-acquired, or force-pushed out from under them.

4b) Fold in the superseded-mid-flight case: codex changes version near-daily, and a new version opens a different branch, so its `agent-maintenance-open-pr` run is in a different concurrency group and runs concurrently with an in-flight acquisition on the previous packet. That run's `Close superseded same-agent PRs` step closes the older packet PR while its acquisition is still going. The branch is not deleted, so the acquire still pushes — onto a packet PR that is now closed. Same root as this item (the watcher acting on a packet that is mid-flight) and the same fix location.

1b) Protection must mean that automation has lost authority to replace this packet generation, never that the packet currently holds a closeout which validates. The late reading still permits the watcher to erase categorization work, a partially authored closeout, publication corrections, or a valid closeout during an intentional edit. Bind the condition to the packet's real identity - agent, target version, and request or run identity - not to the branch name or to the fact that some PR is open.

1c) The condition must also cover a packet that has already merged. A merged packet has no open PR and no closeout artifact, so every open-PR-shaped signal misses it, and the queue still reads the version as needed because the validated pointer only advances at promotion. Observed 2026-09-20: PR #215 merged codex 0.155.0 to staging by accident without promotion, so the branch is reset to a staging that already contains the packet and the re-applied packet diffs only in regenerated timestamps. Expect a content-free packet PR each night until the pointer advances, and test the merged-but-unpromoted case explicitly.

2b) One guard is the right semantic goal, but one early watcher check is not sufficient enforcement. An invocation already queued passes an earlier check and then overwrites later maintainer work, and workflow_dispatch and re-runs bypass the queue entirely. Check immediately before mutation as well, on every destructive path: request regeneration, branch replacement, packet-body replacement, automatic supersession, and closure. Read-only acquisition into non-authoritative artifacts may continue.

2c) Consider an expected-head condition for the branch replacement, so a head that moved since inspection rejects the update. Note the feasibility constraint: the push is performed by peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8, which owns its own push, so this cannot be a --force-with-lease flag on our side and has to be a separate check before the action runs. An expected-head check proves nothing about whether overwriting the inspected content was authorized, so it supplements the ownership predicate rather than replacing it. The repository's existing concurrency group is likewise a supplement: only workflows in the same group participate.
2d) Account for executions already queued or running under the old unguarded workflow when this lands. Merging a guard does not make those safe retrospectively.

6) Do not resolve the request-hash problem by excluding request_recorded_at from the digest. That hides one mutation while leaving force-push erasure and every other request rewrite intact. The invariant is that a request generation's bytes stay stable while that generation is active, and that an intentional request change is an explicit lifecycle operation which deliberately invalidates dependent evidence. The protection check itself must not mutate the hashed request as a side effect.
deliverables: A decided stand-down condition carried by the packet itself
Watcher or open-pr guard implementing it, with a contract test
A recorded decision on superseding a stood-down packet
Direct confirmation of whether a committed closeout survives a nightly run
A stand-down condition that survives a merged-but-unpromoted packet
Enforcement at every destructive mutation boundary, not only in the queue

notes: Found 2026-09-19 while deciding whether T3 should render the audit verdict into the packet PR body or a comment. The body is rewritten from the generated pr-summary on every nightly run, which settled that question for a comment and exposed this larger one.
T8 prerequisite. Lands with the closeout-prerequisite group alongside uaa-0045 and uaa-0039; recorded in the acquisition-maintenance-lifecycle spec §8, "Backlog groups that land inside that order".

The nightly refresh is not purely waste: it keeps an open packet's evidence current and continuously rebases the branch onto staging, which is why packets merge without conflict. The fix is a stand-down condition, not removing the refresh.
Related: uaa-0034 asks whether the gate's verdict still describes the tree that gets pushed after a rebase. This item is the reason those rebases happen nightly rather than occasionally.

2026-09-20, widened. The nightly regeneration does not only delete a committed closeout; it invalidates one that was never committed. request_recorded_at is a field inside maintenance-request.toml, request.rs:399 digests the whole file, and closeout/validate.rs:145 rejects a hash mismatch, so a generated closeout stops validating at the next nightly run while sitting untouched on disk. That makes this item a constraint on T6's output being usable, not only a T8 blocker. Recorded at the trigger point under T4 in the acquisition-maintenance-lifecycle spec.

2026-09-20 sequencing: lands first and alone, ahead of uaa-0045 and uaa-0039. The closeout-prerequisite group was first recorded as one landing; it is three merge units, because the items have independent acceptance conditions and this is the only one with a deadline.

Resolved 2026-09-21. A maintainer freezes a packet generation by committing <maintenance root>/governance/automation-stand-down/<version>.toml, naming agent_id, target_version (which must equal the file name), a reason, and at least one of request_recorded_at / request_sha256. crates/xtask/src/agent_maintenance/stand_down.rs reads the directory (maintenance-stand-down-check, exit 3 = frozen), and agent-maintenance-open-pr.yml asks before each destructive boundary: request regeneration, branch and packet-body replacement, and supersession. A false authorization is the only outcome the guard may never produce, so a compile failure, an unreachable base, a missing registry, an unknown agent and any malformed entry all route to do-not-mutate.

2026-09-21, five design choices worth not re-litigating. (1) Ownership predicate, not validity check: a marker whose recorded generation no longer matches the request is reported and still stands automation down, because a request that moved under a maintainer is when they most need automation to keep away. (2) Markers are a sibling of maintenance-request.toml, never a field in it: request.rs:399 digests the whole request file, so a stand-down expressed inside it would invalidate the closeout it protects. (3) One file per frozen generation, named for it: two same-agent packet PRs can be open at once, so a single per-agent file would make freezing the newer packet silently revoke the older one's protection. Naming the file for the generation also makes the match key checkable, so v0.155.0.toml is rejected instead of quietly never matching. (4) A directory that cannot be read in full stands down: every entry is validated, not only the one that might match, because an unknown freeze set is not an authorization. (5) Markers live on the base branch, not the packet branch - the packet branch is inside the add-paths tree that create-pull-request resets and force-pushes, so a marker carried there could be destroyed by the operation it exists to block. Choice 5 is also what makes step 1c work: a merged-but-unpromoted packet has no branch and no open PR, but base carries its packet, so base carries its markers.

2026-09-21, step 4 confirmed directly. On 2026-09-19 PRs #211 and #208 carried commits dated 2026-09-19 08:03-08:08. Re-read 2026-09-21: both now carry commits dated 2026-09-20 08:35-08:40 and no 2026-09-19 commit survives, with target versions unchanged throughout (claude_code 2.1.267 since 09-16, opencode 1.18.30 since 09-15). add-paths covers the whole maintenance root, which is where close-agent-maintenance writes, so a committed closeout is a strict subset of what was observed being replaced.

2026-09-21, deferred with reasons - do not re-open these without new evidence. (a) The expected-head check from step 2c was dropped: peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 owns its own push, so the check cannot be --force-with-lease on our side and must be a separate step, which leaves the same window it was meant to close only a few hundred milliseconds narrower. It supplements the ownership predicate rather than replacing it, and the predicate does the work. (b) A queue-level dedupe in agent-maintenance-release-watch was dropped: it saves a wasted dispatch but is not sufficient enforcement on its own (step 2b), so it would be a second copy of the rule that must stay in step with the one that enforces. A stood-down run is cheap and its notice is useful evidence. (c) close-agent-maintenance was not changed to require a marker: that would change what requires_manual_closeout = true obligates the human to, which the lifecycle spec section 7 puts on the Ask first list. (d) The acquisition-gate step is deliberately left ungated after a stand-down, raised by the Codex review lane 2026-09-21 as an efficiency note rather than a defect: it is non-destructive, it is the step that keeps a compile failure distinguishable from a planner rejection, and the acquire job is already gated on branch_created, so a condition there would add something that can be wrong to save a few cached seconds. (a) through (c) are recorded at the trigger point, in the stand-down subsection under that spec's T8 sequencing.

2026-09-21, step 2d deploy note: merging the guard does not protect runs already in flight. A dispatch that starts after the merge picks up the guarded workflow; one already executing does not. Before beginning the first closeout, confirm no agent-maintenance-open-pr run is in progress for that agent. Recorded in the spec's stand-down subsection.

2026-09-21, adversarial review findings folded in before the PR opened. Two changed the design. (i) Both guards originally read the same job-start checkout, so the pre-replacement re-check could not produce a different answer than the first check for any reason a maintainer can cause - and the code comment claimed otherwise. create-pull-request resets the packet branch to current base, so the real exposure is the job's whole duration. The re-check now fetches base and reads through --from-ref, where any git failure is an internal error rather than an absent marker. This also restates the expected-head omission honestly: what remains is the seconds between that fetch and the action's own push, not a window the check could have closed. (ii) An unanswerable guard used to leave the job green with no PR, because ::error annotates without failing a step - so a flag rename or one malformed entry could stop every maintenance packet for weeks with nothing going red. Exit 3 still exits green; every other exit now fails the job. Also folded in: strict MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH on the marker's name, and per-generation files (design choices 3 and 4 above), both of which closed silent-authorization paths.

2026-09-21, contract-test quality. The first version of the c4 assertions counted occurrences of stand_down=true/false, which a straight swap of the two branch bodies left unchanged - an inverted guard that force-pushes exactly when a maintainer has frozen the packet passed them. Supersession's continue was also satisfied by two unrelated continues already in the loop, and the unconditional-recheck assertion sliced from `id:` rather than the step header, so an `if:` written above `id:` fell outside it. All three are fixed and the suite is mutation-tested against eight rewrites of the workflow, every one of which it now catches. Re-run that matrix before changing these assertions.

2026-09-21, merged as PR #219 (6e8bfe0d). Follow-ups split to uaa-0050: the acquisition path an agent actually follows, the supersession boundary's stale read, and marker retirement at promotion. This item covers the mechanism only.

items.title: A generic engine branches on the codex agent id to grant an extra writable surface

prompt: Work item: uaa-0049 — a generic engine branches on the codex agent id to grant an extra writable surface.

Context: `crates/xtask/src/agent_maintenance/contract_policy.rs` builds each packet's `writable_surfaces` from registry data, then appends one path behind a hardcoded agent-id test: `if entry.agent_id == "codex" { writable_surfaces.push("docs/specs/codex-wrapper-coverage-scenarios-v1.md") }`.

Why it matters: AGENTS.md and the lifecycle spec both require that agent-specific behaviour live in committed descriptor data, not in generic engines. The parity workflows now hold to that — `parity-acquire.yml` and `parity-promote.yml` contain no agent-specific logic, only `(e.g. codex)` in input descriptions — so this is one of the last places the rule is broken, and it is broken in the engine that decides what a packet is allowed to write.

Impact today is small: codex packets may write one extra spec file that other agents may not. The cost is the precedent. A second such branch would be easy to add and hard to find, and `writable_surfaces` is a permission boundary rather than a convenience.

Distinct from the relay-host constants in the same file (`LEGACY_EXECUTOR_ALIAS`, the `@codex` PR-body mention, the `codex-validate` command name). Those name codex as the local relay execution host, which the lifecycle spec's verified-state table records as intentional design and §4 lists as deliberately untouched. This item is about codex as a maintained agent.
Steps:
1) Decide where the surface belongs: a per-agent `writable_surfaces` extension in the registry, or in the agent's RULES.json alongside the other descriptor data.
2) Move it there and delete the branch.
3) Add a test that fails if any generic engine tests an agent id literal, or at minimum that codex's writable surfaces come entirely from descriptor data.
4) Audit the rest of `contract_policy.rs` for other agent-id tests while in there.
deliverables: The extra writable surface declared in descriptor data
The agent-id branch removed from the engine
A test binding writable surfaces to descriptor data

notes: Found 2026-09-19 while checking whether anything codex-specific survives the parity generalization. The answer: the reusable lanes are clean and all three maintained agents now carry dispatch_kind = "packet_pr", but this branch and the per-agent jobs in ci.yml are not.

Related but out of scope here: ci.yml still hand-writes per-agent validate jobs (a codex-validate-artifacts job, a separate claude_code manifest-validate step), so enrolling an agent still means editing that workflow. Worth its own item if the generalization is meant to reach CI.
Not the relay host. codex as the local execution host for the uplift relay is intentional; see the lifecycle spec's verified-state table and §4 'Deliberately untouched'.

items.title: The stand-down guard has no acquisition path, its supersession boundary reads a stale checkout, and a marker never retires

prompt: Work item: uaa-0050 - complete the packet stand-down landed by uaa-0048 (PR #219, merged 2026-09-21 as 6e8bfe0d).

Context: uaa-0048 shipped the ownership predicate (crates/xtask/src/agent_maintenance/stand_down.rs) and three guards in .github/workflows/agent-maintenance-open-pr.yml. It deliberately stopped at the mechanism. Three things it did not settle are now decided; the reasoning is in the acquisition-maintenance-lifecycle spec's stand-down subsection under T8 sequencing, which is the authority.

The actor matters and changes the costing. A closeout is performed by a coding agent handed the packet PR, not by a maintainer at a keyboard. That agent already holds git and already pushes to the packet branch, so acquiring a freeze needs no remote-write capability added to xtask - which has never pushed (every Command::new("git") in the crate is rev-parse, log, ls-tree or show). Acquisition is therefore an instruction, delivered where the agent already reads.
Steps:

1) Fix the supersession boundary. It calls maintenance-stand-down-check with no --from-ref while running at the END of the job, so it carries the same job-length stale window that the branch-replacement boundary was fixed for, and it is the boundary that acts on a packet other than the run's own. Fetch base immediately before the supersession loop and read through --from-ref, per candidate. Any git failure stays an internal error, never an absent marker.

2) Use the same fresh-ref mechanism at request regeneration (boundary 1). It is the first step after checkout, but a re-run preserves the original event's GITHUB_SHA, so a fresh checkout is not a current one and step order does not imply freshness. Do not institutionalize a "this checkout is probably recent enough" exception when the shared mechanism already exists.

3) Retire a marker in its own promotion PR. In parity-promote.yml's "Advance pointers and version metadata" step, remove docs/agents/lifecycle/<agent_id>-maintenance/governance/automation-stand-down/<version>.toml for the version being promoted. The step already runs on a staging checkout with contents: write, and the "Open the promotion PR" step has no add-paths, so the deletion rides along with the status flip in one commit. Properties this buys: one commit (a failed cleanup leaves an extra marker; a failed promotion never leaves a missing one), maintainer-merged (automation proposes the unfreeze, never performs it), exactly one version named (a second frozen generation is untouched), and correct timing (versions/<v>.json only reads validated once that PR lands, not when the workflow runs).

4) Render the acquisition step into the generated HANDOFF.md via crates/xtask/src/agent_maintenance/docs.rs, pre-filled with the agent, target version, marker path and that generation's request_recorded_at. HANDOFF already calls itself the canonical contributor execution contract and already renders "the exact closeout command" and "the exact maintained-agent prompt", so this is one more rendered block in an existing slot. Never hand-edit the generated files; change the renderer. The closed contract that close-agent-maintenance regenerates should drop the acquisition step but keep a line saying that closing, pushing, approving and merging do not release the stand-down.

5) State the standing rule in AGENTS.md, beside the existing conditional obligation to run manifest-validate after touching cli_manifests/**. Spend the instruction budget on the four points where an agent's default behaviour is wrong: freeze before substantive judgment work rather than before the closeout command; the marker goes to the base branch, never the packet branch; publish only the marker with git add <path> then a path-limited git commit <path>; never force-push staging, and on a rejected push pull --rebase and retry.

6) Share one marker-TOML construction routine and one marker parser between the HANDOFF renderer and (later) the admission gate's refusal output. Two hand-written copies of the schema is the duplication trap; two consumers of one routine is not.

Output: an agent handed a packet PR is told how to acquire the freeze in the place it already reads, every destructive boundary reads a current base, and a promoted packet's marker retires with its promotion.
deliverables: Supersession and request regeneration both read a freshly fetched base through --from-ref
Marker retirement in parity-promote's pointer-advance step, riding into the promotion PR
An acquisition block rendered into HANDOFF.md by the renderer, never hand-edited
A standing freeze rule in AGENTS.md covering the four counterintuitive points
One shared marker-TOML construction routine, reused by the uaa-0039 admission gate
Contract tests in crates/xtask/tests/c4_spec_ci_wiring.rs for the two fresh-ref boundaries and for retirement

notes: Split out of uaa-0048 on 2026-09-21, after PR #219 merged. uaa-0048 is the mechanism; this is the workflow around it. Sequencing: lands as PR 2 of the closeout-prerequisite group, ahead of uaa-0045 (PR 3) and uaa-0039 (PR 4) - it is small, it touches code that just merged, and uaa-0039's admission gate depends on its shared marker routine.

2026-09-21, the supersession gap is a defect in landed code, found by the adversarial lane's reasoning applied a second time. --from-ref appears once in agent-maintenance-open-pr.yml, at the branch-replacement boundary. Supersession runs after Create PR and reads the job-start checkout, so a marker a maintainer lands mid-job is invisible to exactly the boundary that closes someone else's packet. Smaller blast radius than a force-push - gh pr close leaves the branch, so it is reopenable - but it is the guard failing to honour a marker for the one boundary that acts on a packet other than the run's own.

2026-09-21, why acquisition is an instruction and not a command that pushes. Costing the earlier "have the closeout command write the marker" option assumed a human actor and a new authenticated remote write from xtask, which has never pushed. With a coding agent as the actor that cost disappears: it already has git. What remains is delivery, and the generated HANDOFF.md is a purpose-built channel that already renders exact commands for its other steps. Attaching acquisition to close-agent-maintenance would still be wrong - that command is the end-of-work validator, so it protects nothing that has already been done.

2026-09-21, the four counterintuitive points, recorded so they are not trimmed as verbosity. (a) Freeze before judgment work, not before the closeout command: the request-hash clock invalidates an uncommitted closeout, so local work is exposed from the first adjudication. (b) Marker to base, never the packet branch: a control file for this packet, in this packet's directory, is the most natural thing to commit to the branch the force-push replaces. (c) git add <path> then git commit <path>: the add is required because the marker is always a new file (git commit on an untracked path errors with 'did not match any file(s) known to git'), and the path on commit is what keeps a dirty packet tree out; verified 2026-09-21 in a scratch repo. (d) Nothing but retirement releases the freeze.

2026-09-21, no worktree in the happy path. An isolated git worktree was proposed to keep packet work out of the marker commit. It is unnecessary when the freeze happens before any work, which is the whole ordering point, and a path-limited commit is satisfiable by construction where a one-file diff is a property to maintain. Keep the worktree form only in the uaa-0039 admission gate's refusal output, which by construction is read by an agent that already has a dirty tree.

2026-09-21, cleanup is triggered by promotion, never by a new version appearing. The proposal to have the nightly sweep older markers when a new upstream version arrives was rejected: codex ships near-daily and a closeout spans days, so a newer version's first run would delete the marker of the packet being worked on - the supersession hazard this guard exists to prevent, reintroduced as housekeeping. It also makes the restrained party hold the eraser: today the nightly only reads the marker directory, and base is never written by it, which is one of uaa-0048's five load-bearing choices.

2026-09-21, accepted residual with retirement. Once a marker is removed at promotion nothing refuses to rebuild that version: neither agent-maintenance-open-pr nor prepare-agent-maintenance compares a target version against the pointer (prepare.rs:293 reads latest_validated.txt only to confirm it exists, and current_validated arrives as a caller-supplied arg), and the workflow has workflow_dispatch with target_version as a free input plus GitHub's 30-day re-run window. The result is a spurious PR that regresses nothing unless merged - loud, not silent - so a writer-side guard refusing a status: validated version is deferred until one is observed. cli_manifests/<agent>/versions/<version>.json is the durable per-version record that guard would read; unlike latest_validated.txt it does not move when a newer version promotes (verified 2026-09-21: codex 0.125.0 reads validated, 0.155.0 reads reported).

2026-09-21, adjudicated against a two-round ChatGPT Pro approach review (.codex/guidance/2026-09-21-stand-down-signal-medium-consult.md). It endorsed the committed base marker over a PR label and over branch-divergence detection, and endorsed this layering; three of its implementation worries were checked against the shipped code and are not present (the request binding cannot become an escape hatch from the freeze, a missing request does not defeat a marker, and no generation path sweeps the control directory). Its one correct prediction was the freshness gap in step 1.

2026-09-21, resolved. All three destructive boundaries now fetch base and read through --from-ref, so none of them answers from the job-start checkout. parity-promote's pointer-advance step removes the promoted version's marker, which rides into the promotion PR with the reported -> validated flip because that step has no add-paths. The acquisition step is rendered into HANDOFF.md by docs.rs and stated as a standing rule in AGENTS.md, and stand_down.rs now owns the one marker renderer, the one path builder and the BASE_BRANCH constant that the generated instruction, the unit tests and the workflow all read. agent_maintenance_prepare follows the rendered instruction end to end - it pastes the marker out of the handoff's own heredoc at the path the handoff names and asks the guard - and the nine-mutation matrix over both workflows catches every rewrite. uaa-0039's admission gate reuses render_marker_toml and marker_relative_path.

items.title: The effective-flags model is applied to the union but not to wrapper-claim matching, so a wrapper flag claimed at a subcommand scope is reported wrapper-only

prompt: Work item: uaa-0051 - globals.effective_flags_model is enforced on one side of the coverage comparison only.

manifest_union normalizes the union by removing a per-command flag whose canonical key already appears in root flags (manifest_union.rs normalize_union_commands). The descriptor states the intent: 'A command's effective flag set is the union of root flags and that command's own flags', and 'Coverage deltas for global flags are reported only under the root path ([])'.

manifest_report does not apply that model to the wrapper side. A wrapper_coverage.json entry that claims a global flag at a subcommand path finds no counterpart at that path in the deduped union, so the row is emitted as wrapper_only - a surface the wrapper claims and upstream does not have. That is false: upstream has it, at root, and the effective-flags model says the subcommand inherits it.

Scope corrected 2026-09-22: one instance, not five. codex ['debug','prompt-input'] --image on 0.155.0. The union has --image as a root flag and lists ['debug','prompt-input'] with zero flags, because the dedupe removed its inherited copy; the wrapper claims --image there; upstream_flag_availability finds the command, finds no such flag on it, and emits wrapper-only. Codex's root --image is not parity-excluded, so crediting the wrapper's subcommand claim against it is correct.

The four opencode rows previously attributed to this item were not instances of it. They were the report correctly signalling that uaa-0052's descriptor defect had deleted surfaces from the union. uaa-0052 reverted that, and opencode is back to zero wrapper-only rows.

Do not reason from upstream_available_on. On a wrapper-only row that field is a fallback, not upstream truth: when upstream has the command but not the flag it reports the command's availability, and when upstream has no command at that path it reports the wrapper's own target set (manifest_report/report/filtering.rs upstream_flag_availability). All 19 of codex 0.155.0's any-scope wrapper-only flag rows take a fallback branch, so the field lists every target on rows that are genuinely hidden upstream. Read the union instead.

This matters to uaa-0039, which makes closeout fail on any wrapper-only row without a recorded category. Under uaa-0039 this row must be adjudicated, and the only honest category for it is 'a discovery bug' - a category that describes the reporting engine, not the surface.
Steps:

1) Credit a wrapper claim at a subcommand path against a root flag of the same canonical key, when globals.effective_flags_model.enabled is true for that agent. Apply it to wrapper-only detection; check whether missing-surface detection needs the mirror treatment or already gets it from the root-scope reporting rule.

2) Decide whether the corrected row disappears from the report or is emitted with a distinguishing field. Disappearing is simpler; a field preserves the evidence that the wrapper claims a flag at a narrower scope than upstream offers it.
3) Regenerate codex 0.155.0's report and confirm ['debug','prompt-input'] --image resolves. opencode needs no re-measurement: its model is disabled by uaa-0052, so it has no rows of this kind.

4) While here, implement or retract the descriptor's 'reporting' clause. manifest_report never reads globals at all, so 'Coverage deltas for global flags are reported only under the root path ([])' is claimed by every descriptor and implemented by nothing. Decide which it is and make the file say so.
Trigger - resolve before uaa-0039's closeout check goes live, so that row is not categorized as a real surface.
deliverables: Wrapper-only detection that honours the effective-flags model
A decision on whether the corrected row vanishes or carries a distinguishing field
Regenerated codex evidence confirming ['debug','prompt-input'] --image resolves
The descriptor 'reporting' clause either implemented or retracted

notes: Found 2026-09-21 while measuring uaa-0045. codex has carried this one instance since its globals model was enabled.

Rescoped 2026-09-22 from five instances to one. The four opencode rows were misattributed: they were caused by uaa-0052, not by this defect. The stated evidence was also wrong - 'the row contradicts itself because upstream_available_on lists every target' does not hold, because that field is a fallback on wrapper-only rows and carries no upstream flag data. The defect itself was re-confirmed directly against codex 0.155.0's union.
Do not resolve this by disabling the global-flag model for codex. The model is correct for codex, whose root command is in parity; see uaa-0052 for why it is wrong for opencode.

Resolved 2026-09-22. `upstream_flag_availability` now credits a wrapper claim at a subcommand path against a root flag of the same key when the agent's effective-flags model is enabled, and reports that root flag's own availability, so a root flag genuinely absent on some target still fails the filter. The credit is gated on the descriptor's own declaration and on a matching root key, both covered by tests. `manifest_report`'s `RulesFile` now declares `globals` as a required field - it was the one stage of the pipeline that could not see the model the union had already been normalized by.

Three decisions taken while implementing, recorded so they are not re-litigated. (1) The corrected row disappears rather than carrying a distinguishing field. The contract defines a wrapper-only row as a wrapper claim the union does not show, and under the model the union does show it, at root - so it is not a wrapper-only row at all. No evidence is lost: codex's wrapper claims --image at root as well, which is already recorded as covered, and a wrapper that claimed a global only at a subcommand would still show the root flag under missing_flags. A new field would also have been a report-schema change. (2) Missing-surface detection needs no mirror. It iterates the union, which after normalization holds a global flag once, at root, and matches it against the wrapper's root claim - verified against codex 0.155.0, where root --image is correctly absent from missing_flags. (3) The descriptor's `reporting` clause is neither implemented in `manifest_report` nor false; it is enforced in two places, the union normalization on the upstream side and this credit on the wrapper side. The clause in all three descriptors now says where, so the next reader does not conclude it is unimplemented.

codex 0.155.0's six coverage reports were regenerated: exactly one row removed from each, ['debug','prompt-input'] --image, nothing added, no other file touched, support-matrix derivation unchanged. Regenerating this packet is in scope where uaa-0045 declined to regenerate opencode's 1.4.11 and 1.14.47: those are promoted history, while 0.155.0 is the reported packet uaa-0039's closeout check will adjudicate, and leaving a row proven false would force exactly the false adjudication this item exists to prevent. Generated with SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pinned, and the result is byte-reproducible from committed inputs.

items.title: opencode's effective-flags model cancels its root parity exclusions, so 345 surfaces are reported nowhere

prompt: Work item: uaa-0052 - a regression introduced by uaa-0045 in PR #222 and resolved on 2026-09-22.

uaa-0045 enabled globals.effective_flags_model for opencode. That model is incompatible with opencode's parity exclusions, which remove the root command and all 20 of its flags because the root command starts the interactive TUI.

The two cancel. normalize_union_commands deletes every subcommand copy of a root flag from the union. The model's reporting clause says the surviving coverage delta is reported at the root path. That path is parity-excluded. So the surface is reported under no delta list at all - not missing_*, not excluded_*.

Measured by rebuilding the pinned packet (automation/opencode-maintenance-1.18.30 @ 962329a1) with the model on and off: missing_flags 394 to 49, excluded_flags 20 both ways, wrapper_only_flags 0 to 4. All 345 removed rows are subcommand copies of the 20 parity-excluded root keys; none appears under any delta. Each of those 20 exclusion units carries the note 'where a subcommand accepts the same flag, that copy stays in parity' - the exact policy the dedupe inverts.

Resolution: set enabled=false in cli_manifests/opencode/RULES.json, keeping the block declared so the descriptor still states its stance; add a manifest-validate guard refusing enabled=true when the root command is parity-excluded; correct the records that carried the wrong reading.
deliverables: opencode's effective-flags model declared and disabled, with the reason recorded in the descriptor
A manifest-validate guard refusing the model when the root command is parity-excluded
uaa-0051 rescoped, uaa-0039's pointer corrected, uaa-0045 annotated

notes: Found 2026-09-22 by a read-only side session reviewing the merged PR #222, and confirmed by rebuilding the pinned packet both ways.

The root cause is not the model, which is correct for codex and claude_code. It is that a structural switch was used where the auditable mechanism is parity_exclusions, whose own contract is that an excluded unit stays visible under excluded_* with a category and a reason. The switch leaves no row.

The suppressed rows are real work items, because opencode's wrapper covers one command. Suppressing them is a coverage decision, and it belongs in parity_exclusions. Doing it per unit is 345 hand-written entries today, which is why an exclusion form covering a path pattern is the enabling change - see uaa-0055.

items.title: opencode's wrapper covers one command, so 481 upstream surfaces are unwrapped

prompt: Work item: uaa-0053 - build out opencode's wrapper coverage.

cli_manifests/opencode/wrapper_coverage.json holds one entry: run, with six flags and one positional argument, generated 2026-04-18 at wrapper_version 0.2.3. Its note bounds coverage deliberately: 'OpenCode v1 wrapper coverage is intentionally bounded to the canonical run --format json surface.' codex declares 87 command entries and claude_code 30.

The consequence is measurable rather than theoretical. Against opencode 1.18.30 the coverage report holds 481 missing surfaces (60 commands, 394 flags, 27 args). opencode's support-matrix rows read backend_support unsupported on all 18, uaa_support unsupported on all 18, and manifest_support supported on 1 of 18. latest_validated is 1.4.11 while upstream ships 1.18.31.

So opencode is wired into the measuring half of the lifecycle - packets open, help is scraped, reports generate - and has never been built out on the wrapping half. The 481 is the accurate size of that gap, and it is this item's work list.

Sequencing decided 2026-09-22 by the maintainer: this is the destination, not the current work. The acquisition-maintenance lifecycle spec is the priority because it is what makes agent onboarding and maintenance repeatable. This item must not be pulled onto that critical path, and the lifecycle spec's T4-T8 must not wait for it.
Steps:

1) Decide the target surface. Wrapping all 61 commands is one end; wrapping the non-interactive subset that the UAA backend can actually drive is the other. The decision belongs with the backend, not with the manifest.

2) Extend the wrapper and its coverage declarations together. opencode's coverage entries populate no scope.target_triples today, unlike claude_code's 21; decide whether opencode needs target scope as it grows.
3) Advance latest_validated as coverage lands, through the normal promotion lane. Do not hand-edit pointers.
4) Retire uaa-0055's need, or use it: whatever remains deliberately unwrapped becomes parity exclusions with a category and a reason, not a suppressed number.
deliverables: A decided target surface for the opencode wrapper

items.title: A root-flag parity exclusion under an enabled effective-flags model silently deletes subcommand copies

prompt: Work item: uaa-0054 - the narrower half of uaa-0052, left unguarded on purpose.

uaa-0052 added a manifest-validate guard refusing globals.effective_flags_model.enabled=true when the root command is parity-excluded. A root-path *flag* exclusion is the same hazard one step narrower: the model deletes that flag's subcommand copies from the union, and the root copy that would carry the report is excluded, so those copies are reported nowhere.

codex carries one such exclusion today - a root-path --no-alt-screen exclusion, category tui - with the model enabled. It costs nothing at 0.155.0 because no subcommand repeats that flag, so the hazard is latent rather than biting. Deciding the case needs the union, which manifest-validate does not read, which is why it was filed instead of guarded.
Steps:

1) Decide where the check belongs. manifest_union has the union and could refuse precisely - model enabled, root flag excluded, and some subcommand actually carries that flag. manifest_validate can only refuse the descriptor pair, which would reject codex's harmless declaration.
2) Implement it there, with a test using a synthetic descriptor rather than a live agent's.
Trigger - resolve before any agent's subcommand repeats a parity-excluded root flag, or before a second agent adopts a root-flag exclusion under an enabled model.
deliverables: A check that refuses the combination where it is actually harmful
A test that does not depend on a live agent's descriptor

notes: Split out of uaa-0052 on 2026-09-22 rather than guarded there, because the strict descriptor-level guard would have rejected codex's current, harmless declaration.

items.title: parity_exclusions cannot cover a path pattern, so suppressing a repeated global costs one entry per subcommand

prompt: Work item: uaa-0055 - give parity_exclusions a way to exclude one surface across many paths.

Today an exclusion unit names one exact (path, key) pair; manifest_report/report/parity.rs indexes them that way. Excluding --help on all 61 of opencode's subcommands is therefore 61 entries, and excluding the five repeated globals is 305.

That verbosity is why uaa-0045 reached for globals.effective_flags_model instead, which deletes the rows with no record at all - the defect uaa-0052 reverted. The lesson is not that suppression is wrong but that the auditable mechanism was too expensive to use.

An exclusion form that covers a path pattern - all subcommands, or a named subtree - would keep the contract opencode's RULES.json already states, that 'excluded units remain visible in reports under excluded_* deltas and never appear under missing_* deltas', while costing one entry with one category and one reason.
Steps:

1) Design the form. A wildcard path, an applies_to: all_subcommands marker, and an explicit list are the obvious candidates; prefer whichever keeps the report's excluded_* rows enumerable per concrete surface, since the adjudication under uaa-0039 works on concrete rows.
2) This changes the RULES.json schema, which the acquisition-maintenance lifecycle spec section 7 puts on the Ask first list. Get the decision before implementing.
3) Implement in the exclusions index and the report, with tests covering a pattern that matches nothing and one that matches a surface also excluded exactly.
deliverables: A decided exclusion form covering a path pattern
Implementation keeping every suppressed surface visible under excluded_*
A maintainer decision recorded, since this is a RULES.json schema change

notes: Raised 2026-09-22 out of uaa-0052. It is the enabling change for uaa-0053 step 4 and for any future agent whose CLI repeats its globals.
Not on the lifecycle spec's critical path. uaa-0039 needs concrete excluded rows, which this preserves either way.
